newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - NZ budget disappoints economists.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - NZ budget disappoints economists.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Thursday delivered the coalition government's first budget.
The following are economists' initial reactions to the document.
PAUL STEWART, CHIEF ECONOMIST ANZ BANK
"The numbers are at the lower end of expectations and a little disappointing in that regard.

"The operating surpluses are at the low end of market expectations, the bond programme is a little higher than the market would be anticipating, and I think the reaction will be slightly negative as a result of that.
"I think the more concerning feature is the way there's been quite a significant shift in emphasis to the way fiscal risks are managed.

"Under previous administrations there was very strong commitment to running operating surpluses and repaying debt. The emphasis has now shifted much more towards spending and there's much less emphasis on debt reduction.
"That's fine in its own right, but it means that there is significant risk that in the future the fiscal position will deteriorate further and will be back closer to balance or deficit."
Stewart said the government had "certainly taken a significantly different approach to the management of fiscal risk".

"There's much stronger commitment to higher spending, or maintaining the spending programmes that they've outlined, that I think would have been the case in the past if there was, and is, an underlying deterioration in the economic fundamentals.
"I think the market will look at this with a little bit of concern because it does raise the risk that there will be a greater deterioration in the fiscal outlook than otherwise."

"The operating surplus forecast for the coming year I think is a bit less than the market was expecting, even after the Treasurer's comments of last week, so I'd put that slightly on the negative side.

"On the economic assumptions, the growth forecasts are certainly at the upper end of market expectations, but not unrealistic. The inflation numbers possibly are a bit low, however, and that would have the effect of putting a downward bias on welfare benefit spending.
"So overall, probably slightly worse than the market was expecting, but not horribly so."

Alexander said if the government stuck to its intended $5 billion extra spoending over three years but the economy grew at a slower rate than projected, there was a risk that the forecast surpluses would not eventuate.

"I think the risk is, yes, if there is some (growth) outcome like that, and the government said 'we're going to spend $5 billion regardless', and they're saying that now as we've seen, that I think is a bit on the irresponsible side.
"There's definitely fiscal risk in there, but to say that it's something nasty and bad I think is not the case.

"We're still running surpluses, so that's a good cushion, the government's debt is still going down, not as fast as many of us would like to see and not as big a cushion as we would like to see, but overall I think it's really only slightly worse than one was expecting."
